strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and timely problem: exploratory causal effect discovery from high-dimensional RCT data using foundation models and sparse autoencoders, which is a novel and potentially useful direction.

It formalizes a distinction between rationalist and empiricist causal inference and proposes Neural Effect Search (NES), a recursive stratification procedure that attempts to disentangle leaked effects in SAE codes.

The semi-synthetic CelebA benchmark is reasonably designed, with ground-truth attributes, multiple sample sizes and effect magnitudes, and comparisons against t-test, FDR, Bonferroni, and top-k baselines.
The paper provides theoretical analysis, including a consistency result for NES under explicit assumptions, which is more than many empirical papers in this space.
The real-world ISTAnt application demonstrates that the pipeline can be run end-to-end on a scientific trial and recover a known grooming-related neuron, showing practical feasibility.
The authors include reproducibility details for SAE training and promise code release, and they discuss limitations such as data sufficiency and SAE identifiability.
weaknesses: The central 'paradox of exploratory causal inference' is largely a restatement of the well-known fact that with enough power any non-zero effect becomes statistically significant. The null hypothesis being rejected for entangled neurons is not a statistical error but a mismatch between the tested null and the scientific question of interpretability; the theorem is therefore close to trivial.

The consistency proof for NES relies on strong and unverified assumptions, especially the existence of a distinct dominating principal neuron per effect (Assumption A.2) and bounded leakage after conditioning on post-treatment SAE codes (Assumption A.3). These assumptions are not empirically validated and may fail for realistic SAEs.

The method effectively identifies only one principal neuron per effect factor, not the full set of affected codes. If a causal effect is distributed across multiple neurons, NES will miss parts of the effect subspace, which is a significant limitation for the stated goal of discovering unknown effects.

The real-world trial evaluation is weak: no multiple-testing correction is applied due to small sample size, so the reported significance of the two returned neurons is not controlled at any nominal level. One of the two effects is a background artifact, and the other has a low F1-score (0.398), undermining the claim of 'first successful unsupervised causal effect identification.'

The semi-synthetic ground truth is defined as the single most predictive neuron per concept, which is a heuristic that may bias evaluation toward NES and does not account for distributed or multiple-neuron representations of the same effect.

Novelty of the statistical machinery is limited: NES is essentially greedy conditional testing with residualization/stratification, related to recursive feature elimination, orthogonal matching pursuit, and conditional independence testing. The novelty lies mainly in applying this to SAE codes.

The real-world experiment shows no new scientific discovery; it recovers a known grooming behavior and a nuisance background effect. There is no quantitative comparison against baselines on the real dataset or estimate of how many true effects are missed.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, e.g., 'first successful unsupervised causal effect identification' and framing the background artifact as a strength rather than a limitation of the small-sample design.
Minor clarity and presentation issues: title misspelling ('SAENCE'), notation inconsistencies, dense exposition, and pseudocode errors such as 'S=S.append(j)' which returns None.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: exploratory causal inference from high-dimensional RCT data by combining foundation models, sparse autoencoders, and causal inference.
Proposes a concrete pipeline (FM -> SAE -> NES) and a recursive testing algorithm intended to mitigate leakage/entanglement in neural representations.
Provides some theoretical analysis of the multiple-testing issue and NES consistency under stated assumptions, along with semi-synthetic experiments.
Includes a real-world application to an experimental ecology trial and discusses limitations and ethical considerations.
Reports useful implementation details such as SAE hyperparameters, datasets, and a Python code snippet.
weaknesses: The 'paradox of exploratory causal inference' is essentially trivial and misleading: as sample size or effect magnitude grows, any truly nonzero coordinate effect will be rejected by consistent tests, regardless of Bonferroni. Multiple-testing correction controls false positives, not true positives. The real issue is semantic relevance/interpretability, not a statistical collapse.

NES consistency relies on very strong, unrealistic assumptions: full-rank sufficiency, principal-max alignment, bounded leakage/transport error, and exact arm-wise effect decomposition. These are not empirically validated and are unlikely to hold for real SAEs.

The method is essentially greedy orthogonal matching/residualization with Bonferroni gating; novelty over existing sparse recovery and multiple-testing methods is limited, and no comparisons to alternative disentanglement or causal discovery baselines are provided.

The semi-synthetic evaluation uses CelebA attributes and compares discoveries to the SAE neuron that best predicts each attribute. This validates recovery of an attribute-aligned neuron, not recovery of a true causal effect. Baselines are weak (t-test, FDR, Bonferroni, top-k) and omit strong sparse recovery or causal representation baselines.

Real-world validation is weak: only two neurons are returned, one recovers the already-known grooming effect, and the other is a background/design artifact likely due to small sample size. No novel causal effect is discovered, and the procedure relaxes Bonferroni, increasing false positives.

Central claims such as 'first successful unsupervised causal effect identification on a real-world scientific trial' and 'first successful application of sparse autoencoders to causal inference' are overclaimed given the anecdotal real-world evidence and related prior work.

The paper acknowledges that SAE features lack identifiability, so statistically significant neural codes cannot be interpreted as scientifically relevant causal effects without expert post hoc validation. This undermines the main goal of automated causal discovery.

Clarity and writing quality are poor: numerous typos ('SAEnce', 'Y(1) and Y(1)', 'H(Y|X)=0'), inconsistent notation, missing parentheses in algorithms, and a buggy Python snippet (e.g., S.append(j) returns None).
Reproducibility is incomplete: standalone code is promised only for the final version, and some experimental details (data splits, seeds, full SAE training procedures) are missing.
The focus on discrete outcomes due to limitations of continuous SAE concepts restricts applicability and leaves continuous scientific outcomes unaddressed.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem framing: the paper formally distinguishes 'rationalist' vs. 'empiricist' causal inference and introduces Exploratory Causal Inference (ECI), a genuinely interesting setting where the affected outcome Y is unknown and must be discovered from high-dimensional measurements.

The 'Paradox of Exploratory Causal Inference' is a clean, useful conceptual contribution: the observation that increased test power (larger n or τ) causes standard multiple-testing procedures to flag all entangled neurons as significant is formalized in two theorems (3.1, 3.2) and illustrated numerically, providing a clear diagnosis of a real problem.

Neural Effect Search (NES) is a novel and sensible algorithm: recursive stratification on already-discovered neurons to peel off principal effects one at a time is a principled way to handle entanglement, and it is well connected to the multiple-testing and disentanglement literatures. A consistency result (Theorem 4.1) is provided with a reasonably detailed proof sketch.

Good experimental coverage on the semi-synthetic side: a controlled CelebA benchmark with known ground-truth concepts, comparisons against t-test, FDR, Bonferroni, and top-k, evaluation across sample size and effect magnitude, plus ablations on zero-effect, testing rule (Bonferroni/FDR/t-test), and estimator (AD vs. AIPW). NES consistently dominates on Precision/IoU while matching Recall.

The paper is well-written, the pipeline figure is informative, and the relationship to prior work (causal feature learning, causal abstractions, SAE interpretability, heterogeneous treatment effect estimation) is clearly positioned. Limitations, ethics, and reproducibility are explicitly addressed, and code is provided.

Demonstrating the pipeline on a real randomized ecology trial (ISTAnt) with DINOv2 + SAE, recovering the known grooming effect (top predictive neuron, F1=0.398) is a meaningful proof-of-concept that the approach can operate end-to-end on real scientific data.
weaknesses: The real-world validation is thin and partially circular: only a single trial (n=44 videos) is analyzed, NES returns only two neurons, one of which is a background/palette artifact attributed to small-sample imbalance. The one scientifically meaningful neuron (grooming) merely reproduces what prior rationalist analyses already established, so the claim of 'first successful unsupervised causal effect identification on a real-world scientific trial' is stronger than what the evidence supports. Bonferroni correction is abandoned in this experiment due to small n, weakening the statistical guarantees that are central to the method.

The consistency theorem relies on strong, hard-to-verify assumptions (A.1 full-rank V, A.2 principal alignment + global principal-max, A.3 ε-leakage with Γ > 2ε margin). These encode much of the desired behavior (a distinct dominant neuron per effect) rather than deriving it, and the paper does not empirically test how often they hold or how NES degrades when they are violated (e.g., effects with similar magnitudes, overlapping leakage, non-linear code–outcome maps).

The FM sufficiency assumption and the linear representation hypothesis are asserted rather than validated. The paper acknowledges SAE identifiability is open, but the core claim that significant SAE codes correspond to genuine effects rests on this; there is no quantitative assessment of how far the pipeline is from sufficiency/identifiability on either dataset.

The semi-synthetic benchmark uses very simple binary CelebA attributes (eyeglasses, hat, smiling) that are likely near-monosemantic in SigLIP features, potentially overstating NES's ability to disentangle in realistic scientific settings with many weak, overlapping effects. No comparison against actual competing methods for effect discovery (e.g., CFL or causal representation learning baselines) is performed empirically — only discussed in related work.

Practical significance is unclear: the method identifies 'statistically significant' signals that are explicitly not claimed to be scientifically relevant, and even the authors frame it as a 'rescue system' for hypotheses. It is not shown that ECI actually surfaces something a rationalist pipeline would have missed (i.e., the Matthew-effect motivation is not empirically demonstrated).

Minor issues: the title contains a typo ('SAEnce'); the assumption that T is not visible in X and that some W may only affect X is handled loosely; the recursion/stratification computational cost (re-testing all m neurons each round, m=9216) and its scalability are not discussed.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and underexplored problem: discovering *what* is affected by a treatment (unknown outcome Y) rather than the well-studied *who* (heterogeneous effects over covariates W). The rationalist-vs-empiricist framing is conceptually valuable and well-articulated.

The 'Paradox of Exploratory Causal Inference' is a real and insightful observation, formalized in Theorems 3.1 and 3.2: as n or τ grows, any multiplicity-corrected test (even Bonferroni) will eventually flag all entangled neurons as significant, collapsing interpretability. This cleanly motivates the need for the proposed method.

Neural Effect Search (NES) is an intuitive and reasonable procedure: recursively select the strongest effect, then stratify/residualize on already-selected codes to peel off one principal effect per round. The consistency proof (Theorem 4.1) with explicit assumptions (A.1-A.3) is structured and mostly sound.

The empirical study is thorough: a controlled semi-synthetic CelebA benchmark with known ground truth plus a real ecology trial, complemented by extensive appendix ablations (foundation model, SAE dimension, nonlinearity, seeds, testing rule, residualization, ATE estimator, SCM structure, propensity score, and additional baselines).

The authors are commendably candid about limitations (sufficiency, linear representation hypothesis, SAE identifiability) and appropriately position the method as a 'rescue system' for hypotheses rather than a replacement for rationalist inference.
weaknesses: The method's validity rests on a stack of strong, untestable assumptions - FM sufficiency, linear representation hypothesis, and especially SAE identifiability/monosemanticity. The paper's own related-work section cites a 'growing body of negative results' showing SAEs can yield spurious interpretability and fail to isolate atomic concepts, which is in direct tension with the assumption that SAEs recover approximately monosemantic, principal-aligned channels. Without identifiability, the guarantees are largely vacuous in practice.

The real-world validation is thin and only weakly supports the headline claim of 'the first successful unsupervised causal effect identification on a real-world scientific trial.' The trial has only n=44 videos, NES is applied *without* the Bonferroni adjustment that is central to the method (an ad hoc deviation), and of the two returned neurons one (code 550) is a spurious finite-sample design artifact (background marking), while the other (grooming, code 394) merely reproduces an effect already established by prior rationalist analysis. This falls short of the strong claim made in the abstract/intro.

Assumption A.2 (global Principal-Max) is close to assuming what the algorithm aims to find (that the population argmax of the code-level contrast is a principal neuron), making the consistency argument somewhat circular. The margin condition Γ > 2ε in A.3 is also strong and unverifiable.

Evaluation contains potential circularity: ground-truth 'affected neurons' are defined as the max-F1 predictors for each attribute, so a method that correctly identifies a genuinely causal neuron which is not the top-F1 one would be penalized. With r=2 the set-based Precision/Recall/IoU are coarse.

Methodological novelty is moderate: NES is essentially recursive conditional testing with post-selection stratification/orthogonalization (akin to g-computation/standardization), and its relationship to existing sequential/forward-selection and conditional-independence testing procedures is not clearly delineated. The baselines (t-test, FDR, Bonferroni, top-k) are largely strawmen; the more relevant comparisons (LASSO/CFL-inspired) are relegated to the appendix.

Positioning against causal representation learning is somewhat overstated: the claim that CRL methods 'cannot discover outcome variables' and thus cannot be applied to ECI is debatable given interventional CRL work that does identify intervention-affected latent components; a more careful comparison would strengthen the paper.

strengths: Timely and novel framing that connects pretrained foundation models, sparse autoencoders, and statistical causal inference into an 'exploratory causal inference' paradigm, addressing a real limitation (the Matthew effect) in scientific discovery from large atlases and RCTs.

The Paradox of Exploratory Causal Inference is a useful and practically relevant characterization of a real issue: with growing power (sample size or effect magnitude), standard multiplicity corrections cannot prevent entangled neurons from being flagged as significant, motivating a targeted solution.

Neural Effect Search (NES) is a concrete, implementable algorithm (with pseudo-code and a Python snippet) that combines recursive stratification with multiplicity control, and the paper provides theoretical analysis and a consistency result under clearly stated assumptions.

The empirical study is broad, including a semi-synthetic CelebA benchmark with known ground truth, a real-world ecology RCT (ISTAnt), and many ablations over encoders (SigLIP/DINOv2), SAE dimension, non-linearity (top-k vs jump-ReLU), seeds, treatment-effect estimators (AD vs AIPW), structural causal models (opposite effects, varying propensity), and additional CFL-inspired baselines.

The real-world ISTAnt demonstration, even if small, shows the pipeline can surface both a scientifically relevant effect (grooming) and a finite-sample design artifact (background marking), which is a reasonable illustration of the intended 'rescue system' use case.

The authors are unusually candid about limitations, explicitly noting the strong sufficiency/identifiability assumptions, the untestability of the alignment assumptions in practice, and the need for expert interpretation before drawing scientific conclusions.
weaknesses: The core theoretical result (Theorem 4.1) relies on Assumptions A.1-A.3, and especially A.2 (principal alignment / Principal-Max), which essentially encode the conclusion that NES will succeed. When these assumptions are violated (as the authors themselves show with jump-ReLU), NES fails; the consistency theorem therefore provides limited independent validation of the method.

The 'paradox' (Theorems 3.1 and 3.2) is a fairly direct consequence of standard asymptotic t-test theory: any nonzero effect becomes significant as n or tau grows, regardless of Bonferroni. Framing this as a 'paradox' overstates the mathematical novelty of the contribution; the real contribution is the algorithmic fix, which is largely heuristic stratification/residualization.

The real-world evaluation is very thin: only n=44 videos, two returned neurons, and the key biological effect (grooming, code 394) has F1 = 0.398 against hand annotations. This is qualitative evidence, not a convincing demonstration of unsupervised causal effect identification at scale.

The evaluation ground truth is defined as the single argmax-F1 neuron per attribute (Eq. in Appendix D.1), which is problematic precisely in the entangled regimes the paper targets; the authors themselves show Wearing_Hat is spread over multiple neurons under DINOv2 and undefined under jump-ReLU, undermining the reliability of the reported Precision/Recall/IoU metrics.

The semi-synthetic benchmark is narrow: only r=2 binary effects, two CelebA attributes, and a co-effect DGP that is essentially a reweighting of the base image distribution. It is a toy setting relative to the high-dimensional atlases (genomes, cancer, cell imaging) that motivate the work.

The method is restricted to discrete/binary outcomes; the authors acknowledge continuous concepts in SAEs are not well understood and leave this to future work, limiting applicability to the scientific domains used as motivation.

The headline claim of 'the first successful unsupervised causal effect identification on a real-world scientific trial' is stronger than the evidence supports, given the small sample, the low F1 for the interpreted neuron, and the fact that one of the two 'effects' is an acknowledged experimental design artifact rather than a genuine biological effect.

NES uses Bonferroni correction at each round with alpha/m, which is extremely conservative; the authors relax it ad hoc in the real experiment, and the empirical behavior of the recursive procedure under its own stated guarantees is therefore not directly validated on the real data.

The paper contains several presentation issues (e.g., the title typo 'SAEnce', inconsistent notation such as Y(1) vs Y(1) in Eq. 1 discussion, mislabeled references), and the positioning against causal representation learning and CFL could be sharpened given that NES is ultimately a multiple-testing heuristic rather than an identification result.

No direct comparison to the natural alternative of simply applying a pre-registered rationalist pipeline (e.g., Cadei et al. prediction-powered causal inference) on the same data, so the claimed practical advantage of the empiricist view over the rationalist one is not empirically quantified.

strengths: Introduces a novel and timely problem: exploratory causal inference, bridging causal inference, foundation models, and sparse autoencoders.
Formalizes the paradox of exploratory causal inference, showing that standard multiple testing collapses as sample size or effect magnitude grows, with theoretical results.
Proposes Neural Effect Search (NES), a simple recursive stratification procedure with consistency guarantees under stated assumptions.

Extensive semi-synthetic experiments on CelebA with multiple baselines and ablations across encoders, SAE dimensions, non-linearities, seeds, and data-generating processes, demonstrating NES's advantage.
Applies the pipeline to a real-world ecology RCT, yielding interpretable discoveries (grooming behavior and a design artifact) that align with domain knowledge.
Clear writing, reproducibility details, code snippet, and ethical discussion.
weaknesses: Relies on strong, untestable assumptions (FM sufficiency, SAE monosemanticity, principal alignment, bounded leakage). SAE identifiability is unresolved; the method's guarantees may fail in practice, as shown by the jump-ReLU ablation.

Real-world validation is limited: n=44, no Bonferroni correction, only two neurons returned, one is a known effect and the other a design artifact; F1 scores are below 0.6. The claim of 'first successful unsupervised causal effect identification' is overstated given the small sample and lack of statistical control.

The theoretical results are relatively straightforward and the consistency proof depends on tailored assumptions; the method is essentially greedy recursive testing/stratification, which may be seen as incremental.

Evaluation is restricted to two binary attributes in semi-synthetic data; no continuous or many-effect scenarios are tested. The 'ground truth' neurons are defined by F1 against attributes, which may not correspond to true causal effect representations.
No comparison to causal representation learning methods (argued inapplicable), and the baselines are mostly standard statistical tests; the added LASSO/stability baselines are heuristic.

The real-world experiment's second neuron is a background artifact due to confounding with treatment assignment in small batches, highlighting the method's susceptibility to design biases and the need for expert interpretation.
The paper does not provide uncertainty quantification for the real-world discoveries under a valid multiplicity correction; relaxing Bonferroni undermines the statistical significance claim.
Method performance depends on SAE hyperparameters and non-linearity; the exclusion of jump-ReLU due to assumption violation suggests fragility.
